description: We are a team of five from psychology, communication, cybersecurity, industrial engineering and product development. We believe heart and mind can’t be looked after separately: stress affects the heart, and cardiovascular health shapes how we feel. Our project explores how to monitor both together to keep astronauts healthy on long missions, where help from Earth is far away. Different backgrounds, one shared goal: caring for the humans who explore space.

details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Inner Ground Control is an app that monitors astronauts’ cardiovascular and psychological health as one connected system. In space, the two are closely linked. Chronic stress raises cardiovascular risk, and changes in blood and circulation can affect mood, sleep and cognitive performance. Most approaches monitor them separately. We look at them together.

The app works in three steps:

  1. Monitor. It receives data from an existing wearable patch, worn on the shoulder, that continuously measures cortisol (a key stress biomarker) and blood viscosity through sweat and skin. The astronaut doesn’t need to do anything extra.
  2. Detect. Using indicators and thresholds, the app spots early signs of risk, such as elevated stress, chest pressure or high blood pressure, before they become a problem. It also shows each crew member’s status in a clear visual interface.
  3. Act. When a risk is detected, the app suggests countermeasures such as guided breathing, brown noise or joint-pressure techniques. Each suggestion depends on three factors: the person, the symptom and the context. The app detects whether the astronaut is alone or with crewmates, and whether they are inside the habitat or outside. It then unlocks only the solutions that make sense in that situation. After trying a solution, the astronaut gives quick feedback on whether it helped, and the app uses that to refine its next suggestions. Over time, the support becomes truly personal.

What benefits does it have?

  • Preventive: it acts on early signals instead of reacting to emergencies.
  • Integrated: it gives a single view of body and mind.
  • Personalised and adaptive: it learns what works for each astronaut.
  • Context-aware: it only recommends what is realistic given where the astronaut is and who they are with.
  • Supports autonomy: it helps crews manage their own health when communication delays make real-time support from Earth impossible.
  • Non-invasive: it collects continuous data without blood draws or interrupting the astronaut’s work.

What is the intended impact?

As missions move towards the Moon and Mars, crews will spend months isolated, confined and far from medical care. Behavioural health and cardiovascular changes are among the key risks of long-duration spaceflight, and one crew member’s health issue can affect the whole team and the mission. Inner Ground Control aims to give every astronaut their own “inner mission control”, a tool to understand, prevent and self-manage health risks before they escalate.

Beyond space, the same approach could support people in isolated, confined and extreme environments on Earth, such as polar stations, submarines or offshore platforms, and in high-stress professions.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

Prototype (software)

  • HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks or build step. Each prototype is a single self-contained file that runs in any browser, which made it easy to share and test during the hackathon.
  • SVG for the watch interface: the mind and heart rings, the curved clock, 7-day sparklines against each astronaut’s own baseline, and the breathing guide.
  • Web Audio API to generate brown noise live in the browser, with no audio files.
  • Atkinson Hyperlegible Next (Google Fonts), a typeface designed for legibility, chosen for a small round screen read under stress.
  • Accessibility built in: keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels and a reduced-motion mode.
  • Simulated data: three scenarios (normal, stress and alert) model the readings, since we had no live sensors.
  • Vercel: deploy.

Hardware (reference, not built)

  • An existing sweat patch worn on the shoulder, as the source of cortisol readings.
  • A smartwatch for HRV, resting heart rate and sleep, and as the main interface, with a crown and a side button for Quick relief.
  • A tablet to run the guided neck ultrasound.

All sensor data in the demo is simulated. The prototype is educational and is not a medical device.

AI tools

  • Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) to help write and refine the HTML prototypes, research sources and draft the project text and slides.
  • ChatGPT to generate the mission patch logo.
  • NotebookLLM for research.

Collaboration and presentation

  • GitHub as a shared repository, so the whole team could work on the HTML files.
  • Google Slides for the presentation, using NASA’s web typefaces: Inter, Public Sans and DM Mono.
  • Magnific for the video showed at the pitch.

How is your project creative?

  • It treats body and mind as one system, not as two separate health domains.
  • It closes the loop. It doesn’t stop at monitoring. It goes from detection to action to feedback, and every cycle makes the next recommendation better.
  • It unlocks solutions by context. The same symptom calls for a different response depending on whether the astronaut is alone in their quarters, working with the crew or outside the habitat.
  • It relies on simple, low-resource countermeasures such as breathing, sound and pressure. They need no extra equipment, which suits missions where every kilogram counts.

What factors did your team consider?

  • A multidisciplinary view: our team combines psychology, communication, cybersecurity, industrial engineering and product development, so we approached the problem from human, technical and design perspectives at once.
  • Astronaut workload: interaction is minimal, with quick feedback and no extra tasks in an already demanding schedule.
  • Feasibility: we integrate an existing patch instead of developing new hardware, so we could focus on the software and the user experience.
  • Data privacy and security: health data is highly sensitive, so we considered how it is protected and who can access it.
  • Individual differences: the same countermeasure doesn’t work for everyone, which is why feedback and personalisation are at the core of the app.
  • Communication delays: the system has to work autonomously, without depending on real-time support from Earth.
